goal: Teach Year-2 physics students to move from a familiar vertical-motion model to named MATLAB variables, sampled arrays, element-wise operations, a labelled plot, and one executable physical validation check.

deck_context.source_summary: This Week 01 lecture repairs uncertain MATLAB foundations through one familiar model: a ball launched vertically upward with air resistance neglected. Students predict the motion, identify variables and units, create a time array, use MATLAB indexing and element-wise operators, plot height against time, and validate the known launch value.
deck_context.core_claim: A physical model becomes trustworthy computational evidence only when its variables, arrays, operations, plot, and validation check stay connected.

slides.title: Physics to Arrays and Plots
slides.intent: Open with one familiar physical story and make the model-to-evidence journey visible.
key_points: A familiar vertical-motion model becomes a computational object.
The route is physical model, arrays, plot, validation, and interpretation.

slides.title: The equation links each term to motion
slides.intent: Make the analytical model readable before translating it into MATLAB.
key_points: y0 is the starting position.
v0 t is the upward contribution.
-(1/2) g t^2 is the gravity contribution.
Every term on the right has units of metres.
slides.local_context: Use y(t) = y0 + v0 t - (1/2) g t^2 with upward positive and air resistance neglected. The final quantity y(t) is vertical position in metres.

slides.title: Names and units keep the model readable
slides.intent: Reduce ambiguity by translating physical quantities into meaningful MATLAB names before code reading.
key_points: Translate t, y, v0, and g before writing code.
Keep units visible in names or comments.
Distinguish variables from fixed parameters.
Readable names support unit checks.
slides.local_context: Preferred MATLAB naming convention is t_s, y_m, v0_mps, and g_mps2. Units are s, m, m s^-1, and m s^-2.

slides.title: Build the time array first
slides.intent: Show that an array is a physical sampling plan with one time value for each computed height.
key_points: t_s = 0:0.1:4; creates 41 samples.
t_s = linspace(0,4,41); creates the same endpoints and count.
length(t_s) reports 41.
MATLAB indexing starts at 1.
slides.local_context: Both code lines represent time in seconds from 0 to 4 s. Use exact MATLAB syntax and readable code typography.

layout.composition: left: two code routes in a single comparison panel; right: sampled time axis with launch and end highlighted; bottom: one short indexing reminder

visual_elements.supporting_elements: two code snippets, 41-sample count, and launch/end markers

slides.source_image_rules: No supplied visual is required; render the exact code as legible teaching typography.
constraints: Preserve punctuation in both MATLAB lines.
Do not add a dense table.

slides.title: An index selects one physical moment
slides.intent: Connect abstract array positions to known moments in the motion.
key_points: t_s(1) is the launch time.
t_s(11) selects 1.0 s.
An index is not a time value.
Read the array position before interpreting the physical state.
slides.local_context: Use the 41-sample time array from 0:0.1:4 s. Make the mapping t_s(1) = 0.0 s and t_s(11) = 1.0 s explicit.

slides.title: Dots tell MATLAB to work through an array
slides.intent: Repair the most important Week 1 syntax misconception by contrasting scalar arithmetic with per-sample array operations.
key_points: 20 * 3 produces one number.
v0_mps .* t_s produces one value for every time.
t_s.^2 squares every stored time value.
The dots make the operation element-wise.
slides.local_context: Use the exact strings 20 * 3, v0_mps .* t_s, and t_s.^2. The central visual should show one time array becoming one output value per sample.

slides.title: The algorithm appears before the MATLAB syntax
slides.intent: Make the ordered computational plan explicit before students trace code.
key_points: Choose the model parameters.
Create an array of times.

Plot height against time.
Check the launch value.
slides.local_context: The five steps operate on the locked vertical-motion model and lead to one labelled height-time plot plus the launch-value validation.

slides.title: Short code should expose the physics
slides.intent: Guide students to locate model parameters, array construction, element-wise calculation, plotting, and checking in a runnable fragment.
key_points: Read comments and variable names first.
Locate the parameters and time array.
Trace the model line with .* and .^.
Locate the plot and boundary check.
slides.local_context: Use this exact code fragment: v0 = 20; g = 9.81; t = linspace(0,4,11); y = v0.*t - 0.5*g.*t.^2; plot(t,y,'LineWidth',2); y(1). Keep comments concise and code readable.

It falls toward the launch height.
Axis labels, units, and title make the output interpretable.

slides.title: A boundary check can reveal an error that a smooth curve hides
slides.intent: Model the minimum executable physical check students should perform before trusting a result.
key_points: The known condition is y(0) = 0 m.
In a one-based array this is y_m(1).
assert(abs(y_m(1)) < 1e-12) makes the check executable.
A smooth graph is not enough.
slides.local_context: The validation compares the computed first array value with the known launch condition. Use a clear passing state and retain the exact assert syntax.
